seo.title: Author Pages for E-E-A-T: What to Include and Why
seo.meta_description: Author pages for E-E-A-T: what to include, how they show expertise to readers and AI, structured data, reviewer credits and common mistakes to avoid.

h1: Author Pages for E-E-A-T: How to Show Who Stands Behind Your Content
answer: Author pages show readers, search engines and AI tools who wrote your content and why they are qualified. A strong author page includes the person's full name, role, relevant experience, credentials, areas of expertise, a photo, links to their professional profiles and the articles they wrote or reviewed. Google's guidance asks who created content; author pages answer that clearly.
key_takeaways: Author pages answer Google's "who created this?" question.
Include experience, credentials and areas of expertise.
Link every article to its author, and the author to their articles.
Use reviewer credits for expert-reviewed topics.
Keep names consistent across your site and profiles.

sections.heading: Why author pages matter
sections.body_html: Google's guidance on helpful content encourages asking who created content, how and why, and says trust is the most important part of E-E-A-T. An anonymous article gives readers no way to judge whether the writer knows the subject. An article linked to a real person with relevant experience does. For AI tools choosing between sources, visible expertise is one of the signals that makes a page a safer choice.

sections.heading: What to include
sections.body_html:
• Full name as used professionally.
  • Role and organization.
  • Relevant experience: years, projects, clients served, with permission.
  • Credentials: licenses, certifications, degrees that matter for the topics.
  • Areas of expertise: the subjects they write about.
  • A real photo.
  • Professional profiles: LinkedIn and other relevant sites.
  • A list of their articles on your site.

sections.heading: Write the bio for readers
sections.body_html: Lead with what makes the person qualified to advise on these topics, in plain language. "Maria has run GEO audits for more than forty service businesses in Southern California and previously led SEO for a regional healthcare group" says more than a list of adjectives. Keep it accurate and specific; exaggerated bios undermine the trust they are meant to build.

sections.heading: Connect authors and articles
sections.body_html: Show the author's name, with a link to their author page, near the top of each article. On the author page, list the articles they have written or reviewed. This two-way connection helps readers explore and helps machines understand which person is responsible for which content. Google's Article structured data documentation supports specifying an author, and the author's name and URL should match what is visible on the page.

sections.heading: Reviewers for expert topics
sections.body_html: For topics that affect health, finances, legal matters or safety, add a reviewer credit: "Medically reviewed by Dr. Jane Lee, DDS" or "Reviewed by a licensed CPA", with a link to the reviewer's page and the date of review. This shows a qualified professional checked the content even when a writer drafted it.

sections.heading: Company authors
sections.body_html: Some content is best attributed to the organization, such as policies or announcements. That is fine, as long as the organization's About page clearly explains who is behind it. For advice and guides, a named person is usually more trustworthy than "Admin" or "Team".

sections.heading: Consistency across the web
sections.body_html: Use the same name, title and photo for each author on your site, LinkedIn, guest articles, podcasts and conference pages. Consistent identity lets readers and AI systems connect an author's work across sites, which builds a recognizable reputation over time.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.body_html:
• Generic "Admin" or "Staff writer" bylines on expert content.
  • Bios with no relevant experience or credentials.
  • Stock photos or invented authors.
  • Author pages that do not link to any articles.
  • Structured data naming a different author from the visible byline.

Invented authors are especially damaging: if discovered, they undermine trust in everything on the site.

sections.heading: Small businesses and solo experts
sections.body_html: A small business may have one author: the owner. That is a strength, not a weakness. A detailed owner bio that explains years in the trade, the kinds of jobs done and why they started the business is exactly the first-hand experience large publishers cannot match.

sections.heading: How to roll it out
sections.body_html:
1. List everyone who writes or reviews content.
  2. Create an author page for each, using the elements above.
  3. Add bylines and links to every existing article.
  4. Add reviewer credits to expert-reviewed topics.
  5. Update Article structured data with author details.
  6. Review bios once a year.

sections.heading: The short version
sections.body_html: Author pages make expertise visible. Name real people, explain why they are qualified, connect them to their work, add expert reviewers where the stakes are high and keep identities consistent everywhere.

sections.heading: An example author bio
sections.body_html: "Daniel Ortiz is the founder of a three-person GEO consultancy in Anaheim. Before starting it, he spent eight years running SEO for regional home service companies, managing websites and listings for more than sixty locations. He writes about local AI search, Google Business Profile and structured data, and reviews every technical guide on this site. He holds Google Analytics certification and speaks regularly at Orange County business events. Connect with him on LinkedIn." Every sentence is specific and checkable, and it explains why Daniel is worth listening to on these topics.

sections.heading: Author pages and AI answers
sections.body_html: When an AI tool cites a page, it may also describe the source: "according to a guide by a licensed CPA" or "an agency that specializes in local SEO". Clear author information makes those descriptions accurate and more persuasive to the person reading the answer.

sections.heading: Author pages for small teams
sections.body_html: If only one or two people write for your site, keep it simple: one detailed author page per person, a byline on every article and a short bio at the end of each post. Update the bios when roles or credentials change, and add new expertise as the person takes on new kinds of work. A small, accurate set of author pages is far better than an elaborate system nobody maintains.

faqs.a: A page on your site about a person who writes or reviews your content, explaining who they are, their experience and credentials, and listing their articles.

faqs.q: Do author pages help with E-E-A-T?
faqs.a: They make expertise and accountability visible, answering Google's question of who created the content. They support trust but cannot fix weak content.

faqs.q: What should an author bio include?
faqs.a: Full name, role, relevant experience, credentials, areas of expertise, a real photo, professional profile links and a list of articles.

faqs.q: Should every article have a named author?
faqs.a: Advice and guides should. Policies and announcements can be attributed to the organization if the About page explains who is behind it.
A note showing that a qualified professional reviewed the content, with their name, credentials, a link to their page and the review date.

faqs.q: Do author pages help in AI search?
faqs.a: They make it easier for AI systems to see who stands behind content, which supports trust in choosing sources.

faqs.q: Can I use a pen name?
faqs.a: It is safer to use real names for expert advice. Invented authors undermine trust if discovered.

faqs.q: Should I add author structured data?
faqs.a: Yes, through Article structured data that names the author and matches the visible byline.

faqs.q: How long should an author bio be?
faqs.a: Long enough to explain relevant experience and credentials clearly, usually a short paragraph on articles and a fuller version on the author page.

faqs.q: Should freelance writers have author pages?
faqs.a: Yes, if they write under their own name. If an expert reviews their work, credit the reviewer as well so the expertise behind the page is clear.
